paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Washington took place near Florence, Howard County, Maryland, in late June 1888, when a Black boy of about ten, accused of cutting the throats of two young white children in his care, was met with threats of lynching after his arrest. No mob formed against him; he was jailed at Ellicott City, tried for murder in September, and acquitted. Papers treated the case as notable chiefly for the age of the accused, whose youth one telegram gave as the reason he was unlikely to suffer mob violence.

Washington lived with R. D. Layton, a tenant farmer about a mile south of Florence, and had often been left to mind the Layton daughters, Sadie, nearly three, and Beulah, about sixteen months. He had come with his mother from Washington two or three years earlier, and he said his name was not Washington but Hawkins.

According to a Baltimore Sun dispatch, on Tuesday afternoon (June 26) the mother was nursing a neighbor and the father was working in sight of the house when the boy came to him and said someone had cut the children's throats. The father found both girls on the bed with deep gashes; the boy at first blamed a man who had fled across the fields, but after the elder girl pointed to him he was reported to have confessed, saying he was tired of minding them.

Layton swore out a warrant before Squire E. M. Owings at Lisbon, and Sheriff George D. Day arrested the boy, who was committed for the grand jury and taken to the county jail at Ellicott City. The Sun dispatch said his mother was "only too glad" to give him to the sheriff because she feared the neighbors' anger would turn to violence. An Ellicott City telegram in the Richmond Dispatch reported that the feeling in Florence was intense and "threats of lynching could be heard on all sides," but judged that, owing to his age, he would probably not suffer mob violence.

Beulah Layton died, and in September Judge Miller asked the Howard County grand jury to examine the case specially, weighing "the enormity of the crime" against the prisoner's youth. At the trial on September 11, the father testified that the morning after the wounding he had taken the boy behind the woodshed with a rope and pretended to hang him to make him tell the truth. The court excluded a confession the mother had drawn out with a promise that no one would hurt him, and on September 12 the jury acquitted him of the murder of Beulah and the attempted murder of Sadie.

The case ran only in the white press in the coverage found. The Richmond Dispatch headlined it "A Human Fiend," compared the act to those of Jesse Pomeroy, called the boy "the young fiend" and "very dark and repulsive-looking," and mentioned the lynching threats in a single sentence. Short wires in western papers such as the Rock Island Argus and the Yankton Press and Dakotaian told of the crime and jailing without the lynching talk.

The trial drew a long Baltimore American account, reprinted in Savannah, that dwelt on the boy's small size and ragged clothes and called him "a veritable brownie." After the verdict the Annapolis Evening Capital wrote that the acquittal left the case "shrouded in mystery" and asked who had done the deed if the boy had not.

Reports differed on the date of the crime, given as Tuesday in the Sun dispatch, as "yesterday" in a June 29 wire, and as June 20 in the doctor's testimony as printed. Early wires said the younger child would die, the Sun dispatch called the dead child Beulah "the eldest," and the trial report and verdict wire named Beulah, sixteen months, as the child who died. The Richmond telegram had the sheriff find the boy on the street at Florence, while the Sun dispatch had him arrested at the Layton house with his mother.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Washington
bases: The only collective action against Washington in the coverage is talk: a Richmond Dispatch telegram reports 'threats of lynching' heard on all sides after his arrest, and a Sun dispatch says his mother feared neighbors' violence; no mob gathered or attacked him (A5, A8).
Washington was not killed: he was jailed, indicted and tried, and was acquitted (A5, A14, A15). The threats were reported as general talk with no group named or action taken (A5, A8).

Only the Richmond Dispatch telegram reports lynching threats (A5); the Sun dispatch's report of the mother's fear of neighbors' violence partly supports it (A8), while the crime, arrest and acquittal are reported by several independent papers (A6, A8, A14, A15).

accounts.label: Ellicott City telegram (Richmond Dispatch)
accounts.gist: Washington, 'with a reputation for viciousness', cut both children's throats while the parents visited a sick friend; the sheriff found him on the street, he confessed, and threats of lynching were heard on all sides.

accounts.label: Baltimore Sun dispatch from Mt. Airy
accounts.gist: The father was hoeing tobacco in sight of the house; the wounded girl pointed to the boy, who confessed and was arrested at the house in his mother's company, she fearing the neighbors' violence.

accounts.label: Trial testimony (Baltimore American)
accounts.gist: The father described a pretended hanging the morning after; the mother told of a confession drawn out with a promise of no harm and $2, which the court excluded.

accounts.label: The boy's own account
accounts.gist: He first said a strange man (in some reports a white man) had cut the children's throats and fled; he later confessed, saying he was tired of minding them.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headlined it 'A Human Fiend', called the boy 'the young fiend' and 'repulsive-looking', reported the lynching threats without comment and predicted no mob violence because of his age.
The Sun dispatch called it 'An Almost Incredible Crime' and stressed the boy's composure and 'bad face'.
Western papers carried short wires ('Looks Like Another One', 'A Child's Crime') without the lynching talk.
After the acquittal the Annapolis Evening Capital wrote that the case was 'shrouded in mystery' and asked who had done it.
